claims.source: Importantly, genetic ACE2-deficiency completely prevented mCOVID-19 development.
claims.evidence: Data from Ace2-/y mice showing maintained body weight, temperature, and absence of lung pathology (Figure 7B-E).

claims.claim: Inhalation therapy with recombinant ACE2 fully protected mice from mCOVID-19.
claims.source: Finally, inhalation therapy with recombinant ACE2 fully protected mice from mCOVID-19, revealing a novel and efficient treatment.
claims.evidence: Experimental data showing protection from weight loss, reduced viral load, and improved survival with rmsACE2 treatment (Figure 7G-O).

claims.claim: Disease severity is determined by cytokine-driven immunopathology and critically dependent on ACE2 in vivo.
claims.source: disease severity is determined by cytokine-driven immunopathology and critically dependent on ACE2 in vivo.
claims.evidence: Combined evidence from cytokine blocking experiments (Figure 6) and ACE2 knockout experiments (Figure 7).

claims.claim: The Q498H mutation appeared immediately after passage 1 and correlated with early increase in viral load.
claims.source: Most prominently, we observed the immediate appearance of Q498H after passage 1 (Figure 2B), which correlated with the early increase in viral load (and hence viral propagation) in infected mice (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Sequencing data showing mutation appearance (Figure 2B) and viral load measurements (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: The Q493R mutation was detected after passage 12.
claims.source: After passage 12, we detected a glutamine to arginine exchange at position Q493R (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Sequencing data presented in Figure 2B showing mutation dynamics.

claims.claim: Mutations at Q493 and Q498 have been reported in other mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains.
claims.source: Importantly, mutations at Q493 and Q498 have been also reported in other mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains (Dinnon et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Leist et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020b), suggesting a critical role in Spike adaptation to the murine ACE2 receptor.
claims.evidence: Citations to previous studies reporting similar mutations.

claims.claim: Q493 and Q498 mutations were detected in the Omicron/B.1.1.529 variant for the first time in a human SARS-CoV-2 variant.
claims.source: With the appearance of Omicron/B.1.1.529, the most recent VOC, Q493, and Q498 mutations were detected in a human SARS-CoV-2 variant for the first time.
claims.evidence: Reference to the emergence of Omicron variant with these mutations.

claims.claim: Mutations in K417 appeared around passage 10 and have been reported in Omicron/B.1.1.529, Beta/B.1.351, and Gamma/P1 variants.
claims.source: Mutations in K417 (which appeared around passage 10; Figure 2B) have also been reported in Omicron/B.1.1.529 and two other human VOCs, that is, Beta/B.1.351 (K417N) (Tegally et al., 2020) and Gamma/P1 (K417T) (Voloch, 2020).
claims.evidence: Sequencing data (Figure 2B) and citations to variant characterization studies.

claims.claim: The surface of mACE2 consists of more negatively charged amino acids than hACE2.
claims.source: Structural analyses of mouse and human ACE2 (mACE2 and hACE2, respectively) have shown that the surface of mACE2 consists of more negative charged amino acids than that of hACE2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Rodrigues et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Structural modeling data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and citation to previous structural analysis.

claims.claim: The maVie16 Spike Q498H mutation strengthens interaction with mACE2 at amino acid D38.
claims.source: Detailed structural modeling of the BavPat1 versus the maVie16 Spike protein interface with mACE2 revealed that the maVie16 Spike Q498H mutation would strengthen its interaction with mACE2 at amino acid D38, otherwise forming an intramolecular salt bridge with mACE2 H353 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Structural modeling predictions shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The arginine at maVie16 Spike position 493 is predicted to interact with the negatively charged mACE2 amino acid E35.
claims.source: Similarly, the newly introduced arginine at maVie16 Spike position 493 is predicted to efficiently interact with the negatively charged mACE2 amino acid E35, thus further stabilizing the maVie16 Spike/mACE2 interaction by neutralizing the otherwise unpaired negative charge of mACE2 glutamic acid (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Structural modeling predictions shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The threonine at Spike position 417 (T417) of maVie16 is predicted to enhance interaction with asparagine at position 30 of mACE2.
claims.source: Finally, the threonine at Spike position 417 (T417) of maVie16's is predicted to enhance the interaction with the neutrally charged asparagine at position 30 of mACE2 while the aspartic acid at this position in hACE2 forms a salt bridge with lysine K417 of the original BavPat1 isolate.
claims.evidence: Structural modeling predictions discussed in the text.

claims.claim: maVie16 showed similar propagation kinetics in Vero and Caco-2 cells as compared to BavPat1.
claims.source: Of note, maVie16 showed similar propagation kinetics in Vero and Caco-2 cells as compared to BavPat1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: In vitro viral propagation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In BALB/c mice, maVie16 at 4 × 10³ TCID50 caused profound weight loss starting around day 3 post infection.
claims.source: In BALB/c mice, maVie16 was highly pathogenic and caused profound weight loss, starting around day 3 post infection (p.i.) at a dose of 4 × 103 TCID50 (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: Body weight data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: All tested higher doses than 4 × 10³ TCID50 in BALB/c mice caused earlier weight loss (day 2 p.i.) and lethality starting at day 4 p.i.
claims.source: whereas all tested higher doses caused an earlier weight loss (day 2 p.i.) and lethality starting at day 4 p.i. (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Survival and body weight data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Loss of body weight correlated with hypothermia in BALB/c mice infected with maVie16.
claims.source: Notably, the loss of body weight correlated with hypothermia (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Body temperature data shown in Figure 3C correlating with weight loss data.

claims.claim: maVie16 infection did not cause lethality nor significant hypothermia in C57BL/6 animals.
claims.source: In contrast to BALB/c mice, maVie16 infection did not cause lethality nor significant hypothermia in C57BL/6 animals
claims.evidence: Survival and temperature data for C57BL/6 mice shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: 1 × 10⁵ TCID50 maVie16 induced profound but transient body weight loss of about 15% in C57BL/6 mice.
claims.source: albeit 1 × 105 (and higher) TCID50 induced a profound but transient body weight loss of about 15% (Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: Body weight data for C57BL/6 mice shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mouse strains infected with 1 × 10⁵ TCID50 showed similar body weight loss (approximately 15%) at day 3 p.i.
claims.source: Interestingly, both mouse strains infected with 1 × 105 TCID50 showed similar body weight loss (approximately 15%) at day 3 p.i., but while disease severity further increased in BALB/c animals, C57BL/6 mice recovered.
claims.evidence: Comparison of body weight data between strains from Figure 3.

claims.claim: BALB/c animals showed more severe lung pathologies compared to C57BL/6 mice at day 3 post infection.
claims.source: In line with these data, BALB/c animals showed more severe lung pathologies compared to C57BL/6 mice, as revealed by histological analyses of lungs on day 3 (Figure 3G and H).
claims.evidence: Histological images and scoring data shown in Figures 3G, H, and I.

claims.claim: Diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by alveolar collapse and septal thickening, was more pronounced in BALB/c mice than C57BL/6 mice.
claims.source: While the cumulative histological score revealed no differences between the strains, diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by alveolar collapse and septal thickening, was more pronounced in BALB/c mice (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: Histological scoring data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: KRT18-hACE2 mice were most sensitive to BavPat1 infection and succumbed to infections at doses of 1 × 10³ or 1 × 10⁴ TCID50.
claims.source: As expected (Oladunni et al., 2020), KRT18-hACE2 mice were most sensitive to infection and succumbed to BavPat1 infections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: Survival data for KRT18-hACE2 mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: BavPat1-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice appeared healthy until day 4 p.i. and then progressively lost weight until day 7, accompanied by hypothermia and death.
claims.source: However, the disease course was profoundly different to that of maVie16-infected wild-type animals. BavPat1-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice appeared healthy until day 4 p.i. and then progressively lost weight until day 7, accompanied by hypothermia and death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
claims.evidence: Body weight and temperature data for KRT18-hACE2 mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claims.claim: Death in KRT18-hACE2 mice most likely results from severe encephalitis due to expression of hACE2 in neurons where ACE2 is normally not expressed.
claims.source: Death in KRT18-hACE2 mice most likely results from severe encephalitis due to expression of hACE2 in neurons where ACE2 is normally not expressed (Hikmet et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Citation to study on ACE2 expression patterns.

claims.claim: maVie16 infection caused severe blood leukopenia on day 2 p.i. with prominent reduction of lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and NK cells.
claims.source: maVie16 (5 × 105 TCID50) infection caused severe blood leukopenia on day 2 p.i. with a prominent reduction of lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and NK cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing blood cell populations in Figure 4A and supplements.

claims.claim: An expansion of peripheral plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) was observed at day 2 p.i.
claims.source: At the same time, we observed an expansion of peripheral plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) (Figure 4B), which are important antiviral effector cells capable of efficient and rapid type I IFN production (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing pDC expansion in Figure 4B and citation to pDC function.

claims.claim: Infection led to substantial pulmonary infiltration with leukocytes paralleling the development of pneumonia.
claims.source: Infection led to substantial pulmonary infiltration with leukocytes (Figure 4C), paralleling the development of pneumonia.
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung leukocyte numbers in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A remarkable infiltration with pDCs in the lungs occurred on day 2 p.i.
claims.source: A closer look at the inflammatory cell composition in the lungs revealed a remarkable infiltration with pDCs on day 2 p.i. (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung pDC numbers in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) transiently accumulated in the lung on day 5 p.i.
claims.source: Conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) transiently accumulated in the lung on day 5 p.i., followed by T helper and cytotoxic T cell infiltration and recruitment of monocytes on day 7 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung cDC numbers in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: T helper and cytotoxic T cell infiltration and recruitment of monocytes occurred on day 7 p.i.
claims.source: Conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) transiently accumulated in the lung on day 5 p.i., followed by T helper and cytotoxic T cell infiltration and recruitment of monocytes on day 7 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung T cell and monocyte numbers in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Lung neutrophil numbers dropped around day 2 p.i. to return to baseline levels over the remaining disease course.
claims.source: The abundance of other analyzed immune cell populations did not change substantially, and lung neutrophil numbers dropped around day 2 p.i. to return to baseline levels over the remaining disease course (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung neutrophil numbers in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Pulmonary NK cells did not significantly expand in the lungs of maVie16 infected C57BL6 mice.
claims.source: Surprisingly, pulmonary NK cells, which fulfill important antiviral functions (Björkström et al., 2021), did not significantly expand in the lungs of maVie16 infected C57BL6 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung NK cell numbers in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and citation to NK cell function.

claims.claim: Rapid induction of type I IFN-inducible genes (Eif2ak2 and ifit1) occurred in line with early lung pDC accumulation.
claims.source: In line with an early lung pDC accumulation, we found rapid induction of type I IFN-inducible genes, such as Eif2ak2 (protein kinase R/PKR) and ifit1, accompanied by a profound Il6 response
claims.evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: A profound Il6 response accompanied the induction of type I IFN-inducible genes.
claims.source: In line with an early lung pDC accumulation, we found rapid induction of type I IFN-inducible genes, such as Eif2ak2 (protein kinase R/PKR) and ifit1, accompanied by a profound Il6 response
claims.evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The expression of Tnf, Il10, Il1b, and Tgfb peaked between day 5 and 7 p.i.
claims.source: the expression of Tnf, Il10, Il1b, and Tgfb peaked between day 5 and 7 p.i. (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Ifng induction reached a maximum on day 7, coinciding with increased numbers of T cells.
claims.source: The Ifng induction reached a maximum on day 7, coinciding with the increased numbers of T cells that are prominent sources of IFNγ (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Gene expression data (Figure 4D) and T cell numbers (Figure 4C) showing temporal correlation.

claims.claim: Lung weights significantly increased by day 5–7 p.i. in C57BL/6 mice infected with maVie16 (5 × 10⁵ TCID50).
claims.source: In C57BL/6 mice infected with maVie16 (5 × 105 TCID50), lung weights significantly increased by day 5–7 p.i. (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Lung weight data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Lung viral titers peaked at day 2 p.i. and then gradually declined.
claims.source: Lung viral titers peaked at day 2 p.i. and then gradually declined (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Viral load data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Immunohistochemical staining for SARS-CoV-2 nucleoprotein confirmed the initial presence and subsequent elimination of viral particles.
claims.source: Immunohistochemical staining for SARS-CoV-2 nucleoprotein on lung slides confirmed the initial presence and subsequent elimination of viral particles (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 5C showing viral nucleoprotein over time.

claims.claim: Histological analyses revealed progressive interstitial and perivascular infiltration and signs of diffuse alveolar damage, peaking from day 5–7, and resolving by day 14 p.i.
claims.source: Histological analyses of lung tissue revealed progressive interstitial and perivascular infiltration and signs of diffuse alveolar damage, such as alveolar collapse and septal thickening, peaking from day 5–7, and resolving by day 14 p.i. (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Histological images and scoring data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: Vasculitis was observed early after infection (day 2) and resolved at later time points.
claims.source: Interestingly, vasculitis was observed early after infection (day 2) and resolved at later time points (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: Histological observations shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: Most acute inflammatory parameters had returned close to baseline at day 14 p.i., confirming resolution of inflammation.
claims.source: Moreover, most acute inflammatory parameters (including cytokine genes, innate immune cells, and lung tissue weights) had returned close to baseline at day 14 p.i. (Figures 4 and 5A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming resolution of inflammation.
claims.evidence: Multiple data types (cytokine expression, immune cell numbers, lung weights) shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Expansion of pulmonary cDCs and T helper cells occurred by day 5 and 7, indicating onset of adaptive immunity.
claims.source: Onset of adaptive immunity, as indicated by expansion of pulmonary cDCs and T helper cells by day 5s and 7 (Figure 4C), as well as by increased spleen weight on day 7 p.i. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D)
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showing cDC and T cell expansion in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Increased spleen weight on day 7 p.i. indicated onset of adaptive immunity.
claims.source: Onset of adaptive immunity, as indicated by expansion of pulmonary cDCs and T helper cells by day 5s and 7 (Figure 4C), as well as by increased spleen weight on day 7 p.i. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D)
claims.evidence: Spleen weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Significantly increased levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein-specific plasma IgG1, IgG2b, and IgA antibodies were detected on day 14 p.i.
claims.source: was followed by an efficient humoral immune response, reflected by significantly increased levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein-specific plasma IgG1, IgG2b, and IgA antibodies on day 14 p.i. (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: ELISA data showing antibody titers in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mouse strains exhibited a decline in blood leukocytes, including lymphocytes and NK cells, upon infections with maVie16.
claims.source: Both mouse strains exhibited a decline in blood leukocytes, including lymphocytes and NK cells, upon infections with maVie16 (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data comparing strains shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Pulmonary immune cell dynamics did not differ between BALB/c and C57BL/6 strains, except for an expansion of NK cells in BALB/c mice and elevated pDC numbers in C57BL/6 animals.
claims.source: Also, pulmonary immune cell dynamics did not differ between the strains, except for an expansion of NK cells in BALB/c mice, and elevated pDC numbers in C57BL/6 animals (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data comparing lung immune cells between strains in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Higher NK cell abundance correlated with increased pulmonary IFNγ levels in BALB/c mice.
claims.source: Higher NK cell abundance correlated with increased pulmonary IFNγ levels in BALB/c mice, whereas Il1b was slightly higher in C57BL/6 animals 3 days after infection (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: NK cell numbers (Figure 6B) and IFNγ gene expression (Figure 6C) data showing correlation.

claims.claim: Il1b was slightly higher in C57BL/6 animals compared to BALB/c mice 3 days after infection.
claims.source: Higher NK cell abundance correlated with increased pulmonary IFNγ levels in BALB/c mice, whereas Il1b was slightly higher in C57BL/6 animals 3 days after infection (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Gene expression data comparing strains shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Plasma cytokine levels, viral loads, spleen weight, and lung weight were comparable between BALB/c and C57BL/6 mouse strains at day 3 post infection.
claims.source: Plasma cytokine levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), viral loads (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), as well as spleen and lung weight (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) were comparable between the two mouse strains.
claims.evidence: Multiple measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-F showing no significant differences.

claims.claim: maVie16-infected BALB/c mice treated with anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies significantly improved weight loss.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E)
claims.evidence: Body weight data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment decreased lung weights in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G)
claims.evidence: Lung weight data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment decreased viral load in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G), the viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
claims.evidence: Viral load data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment decreased circulating monocyte levels in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G), the viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), as well as circulating monocyte levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C)
claims.evidence: Blood monocyte data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment had only minor effects on body temperature in BALB/c mice.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G), the viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), as well as circulating monocyte levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) while it had only minor effects on body temperature (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Body temperature data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: In C57BL/6 mice, anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment had no effects on body or lung weights, or viral load.
claims.source: In C57BL/6 mice, the same treatment had no effects on body or lung weights, or viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E, G and H)
claims.evidence: Body weight, lung weight, and viral load data from C57BL/6 antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E, G, and H.

claims.claim: In C57BL/6 mice, anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment significantly improved the altered body temperature and circulating leukocyte numbers.
claims.source: In C57BL/6 mice, the same treatment had no effects on body or lung weights, or viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E, G and H), but significantly improved the altered body temperature and circulating leukocyte numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and I).
claims.evidence: Body temperature and blood leukocyte data from C57BL/6 antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and I.

claims.claim: ACE2 is essential for in vivo SARS-CoV infections.
claims.source: We have previously shown (using Ace2 mutant mice) that ACE2 is essential for in vivo SARS-CoV infections (Kuba et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Citation to previous study using ACE2-deficient mice.

claims.claim: Ace2-/y mice were fully protected against infection with 5 × 10⁵ TCID50 maVie16.
claims.source: In contrast to infected littermate control animals, Ace2-/y mice were fully protected against infection with 5 × 105 TCID50 maVie16, maintained stable body weight (Figure 7B) and temperature (Figure 7C)
claims.evidence: Body weight and temperature data from Ace2-/y mice shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: Ace2-/y mice were protected from pneumonia development as indicated by lower lung weight and absence of lung pathology.
claims.source: Ace2-/y mice were fully protected against infection with 5 × 105 TCID50 maVie16, maintained stable body weight (Figure 7B) and temperature (Figure 7C), and were protected from pneumonia development as indicated by lower lung weight (Figure 7D) and the absence of any lung pathology (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Lung weight data (Figure 7D) and histological images (Figure 7E) from Ace2-/y mice.

claims.claim: Complete absence of nucleocapsid-positive cells was observed in lungs of Ace2-/y animals.
claims.source: Resistance to infection was further indicated by the complete absence of nucleocapsid-positive cells in lungs of Ace2-/y animals (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Immunohistochemistry images showing no viral nucleoprotein in Ace2-/y mice in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Similar viral genome copy numbers were detected in both Ace2+/y and Ace2-/y mice, suggesting detection of initial maVie16 input rather than productive infection.
claims.source: In conflict with this observation, we still detected similar viral genome copy numbers in both groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that this was reflective of initial maVie16 input rather than productive infection.
claims.evidence: Viral genome copy number data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: maVie16-infected BALB/c mice treated with rmsACE2 did not lose body weight.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G)
claims.evidence: Body weight data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice developed less hypothermia compared to vehicle-treated animals.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H)
claims.evidence: Body temperature data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice exhibited lower lung weights compared to vehicle-treated animals.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I)
claims.evidence: Lung weight data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice were largely protected from pneumonia.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I), and were largely protected from pneumonia (day 5 p.i.; Figure 7J)
claims.evidence: Histological images from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7J.

claims.claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice had lower lung viral loads compared to vehicle-treated animals.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I), and were largely protected from pneumonia (day 5 p.i.; Figure 7J), had lower lung viral loads (Figure 7K)
claims.evidence: Viral load data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7K.

claims.claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice had fewer blood neutrophils compared to vehicle-treated animals.
claims.source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I), and were largely protected from pneumonia (day 5 p.i.; Figure 7J), had lower lung viral loads (Figure 7K), and fewer blood neutrophils (Figure 7L) than vehicle-treated animals
claims.evidence: Blood neutrophil data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7L.

claims.claim: Fewer SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid-positive cells were found in lungs of BALB/c animals treated with rmsACE2 compared to controls.
claims.source: Further, we found fewer SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid-positive cells in lungs of BALB/c animals treated with rmsACE2 5 days after infection with maVie16 as compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Immunohistochemistry images from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: rmsACE2 treatment of maVie16-infected C57BL/6 mice prevented weight loss and reduced viral load.
claims.source: Similarly, rmsACE2 treatment of maVie16-infected (5 × 105 TCID50) C57BL/6 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) prevented weight loss and reduced the viral load (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G, respectively)
claims.evidence: Body weight and viral load data from C57BL/6 rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G.

claims.claim: rmsACE2 treatment did not affect temperature, lung weight, and blood leukocyte numbers in C57BL/6 mice.
claims.source: Similarly, rmsACE2 treatment of maVie16-infected (5 × 105 TCID50) C57BL/6 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) prevented weight loss and reduced the viral load (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G, respectively) while it did not affect temperature, lung weight, and blood leukocyte numbers (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, H and J, respectively).
claims.evidence: Temperature, lung weight, and blood leukocyte data from C57BL/6 rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, H, and J.

claims.claim: Inhalative ACE2 therapy was fully protective when applied 12 hr post infection.
claims.source: Strikingly, inhalative ACE2 therapy was still fully protective when applied 12 hr post infection (Figure 7M–O).
claims.evidence: Body weight and survival data from delayed treatment experiment shown in Figure 7N and O.

claims.claim: Mice that received inhalation therapy at 24 hr or 48 hr post infection still developed disease but mortality was completely prevented or reduced.

results.result: Serial passaging of BavPat1 through BALB/c mice for 16 passages generated maVie16, a mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strain. Infectivity was established after the first few passages with increasing viral genome copies, while viral load plateaued after passage 3. Progressive weight loss and increasing inflammatory gene expression in later passages indicated enhanced pathogenicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9, C10, C130-C133 provide converging evidence from viral load measurements (Figure 1B), body weight tracking (Figure 1C), and gene expression analysis (Figure 1E) that document the successful generation and progressive adaptation of maVie16. The data show clear temporal progression of adaptation markers.

results.result: Only three Spike RBD mutations (Q498H, Q493R, K417T) in maVie16 enhanced interaction with murine ACE2 according to in silico modeling. These mutations appeared progressively during passaging and are predicted to strengthen Spike-mACE2 interactions by neutralizing negative charges on mACE2 surface. Similar mutations have been reported in other mouse-adapted strains and human VOCs including Omicron.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C11-C17, C134-C136 are supported by sequencing data (Figure 2A-B) showing limited high-frequency mutations, structural modeling predictions (Figure 2D) demonstrating enhanced interactions, and citations to previous studies. The modeling provides mechanistic rationale for observed adaptation, though experimental validation of predicted interactions is not provided.

results.result: maVie16 showed similar propagation kinetics in Vero and Caco-2 cells compared to BavPat1, indicating that mouse adaptation did not compromise infectivity of human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C18 and C137 are supported by in vitro viral propagation data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) showing comparable growth curves in both simian and human cell lines. This demonstrates retained human cell tropism despite mouse adaptation.

results.result: maVie16 induced profound pathology in both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice in a dose-dependent manner. BALB/c mice showed higher susceptibility with lethality at higher doses, while C57BL/6 mice exhibited transient disease with recovery. Both strains showed similar initial weight loss (~15%) at 1×10⁵ TCID50, but BALB/c mice had more severe lung pathology with pronounced diffuse alveolar damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19-C26 are well-supported by comprehensive dose-response data including body weight (Figure 3A, D), survival (Figure 3B, E), temperature (Figure 3C, F), and histological analysis (Figure 3G-I). The strain-specific differences are clearly documented with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

results.result: KRT18-hACE2 mice were most sensitive to BavPat1 infection, succumbing at doses of 1×10³ or 1×10⁴ TCID50. The disease course differed from maVie16-infected wild-type mice, with delayed onset (day 4 p.i.) followed by progressive weight loss, hypothermia, and death, likely due to severe encephalitis from nonphysiological hACE2 expression in neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by survival and clinical data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F) and citation to ACE2 expression patterns. The comparison highlights limitations of the KRT18-hACE2 model and validates the need for maVie16 as an alternative model.

results.result: mCOVID-19 replicated critical aspects of human disease including early lymphopenia (day 2 p.i.) with reduction of lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and NK cells, accompanied by pDC expansion. Pulmonary infiltration showed temporal progression: pDCs on day 2, cDCs on day 5, followed by T cells and monocytes on day 7. Type I IFN-inducible genes (Eif2ak2, ifit1) and Il6 were rapidly induced, while Tnf, Il10, Il1b, and Tgfb peaked days 5-7, and Ifng peaked day 7 coinciding with T cell infiltration.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C30-C41 are comprehensively supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4A-C), gene expression analysis (Figure 4D), and appropriate temporal sampling. The immune response progression mirrors key features of human COVID-19, validating the model's relevance.

results.result: C57BL/6 mice infected with maVie16 (5×10⁵ TCID50) showed increased lung weights (days 5-7), viral titers peaking at day 2 followed by gradual decline, progressive lung pathology (interstitial infiltration, diffuse alveolar damage, vasculitis) peaking days 5-7 and resolving by day 14. Adaptive immunity onset (cDC and T cell expansion, increased spleen weight day 7) was followed by efficient humoral response with anti-Spike IgG1, IgG2b, and IgA antibodies by day 14.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C50 are well-supported by comprehensive longitudinal data including lung weights (Figure 5A), viral loads (Figure 5B), immunohistochemistry (Figure 5C), histological scoring (Figure 5D), and antibody titers (Figure 5E). The data demonstrate complete disease course from acute infection through resolution and adaptive immunity.

results.result: Comparison of BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice at day 3 post-infection revealed similar blood leukopenia and comparable pulmonary immune cell dynamics, except for NK cell expansion in BALB/c mice (correlating with higher pulmonary IFNγ) and elevated pDC numbers in C57BL/6 mice. Plasma cytokines, viral loads, and organ weights were comparable between strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by side-by-side comparison data (Figure 6A-C, supplements) showing strain-specific differences in NK cells and IFNγ levels while other parameters remained similar. This identifies potential mechanisms underlying differential susceptibility.

results.result: Inhibition of IFNγ and TNF with neutralizing antibodies substantially reduced immunopathology in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice (improved weight loss, decreased lung weights, viral load, and circulating monocytes) but had only minor effects on temperature. In C57BL/6 mice, the same treatment had no effects on body/lung weights or viral load but improved temperature and circulating leukocyte numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C56-C62 are supported by antibody treatment experiments (Figure 6D-G, supplements) showing strain-specific therapeutic effects. The differential responses between strains suggest distinct pathogenic mechanisms, though the lack of effect on some parameters in C57BL/6 mice indicates incomplete understanding of disease drivers.

results.result: Genetic ACE2-deficiency (Ace2-/y mice) completely prevented mCOVID-19 development, with mice maintaining stable body weight and temperature, showing no lung pathology or nucleocapsid-positive cells. However, similar viral genome copy numbers were detected in both Ace2+/y and Ace2-/y mice, likely reflecting initial viral input rather than productive infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C63-C67 are strongly supported by data from Ace2-/y mice (Figure 7B-E, supplement 1B) showing complete protection from disease despite detection of viral RNA. The interpretation that detected RNA represents input virus rather than replication is reasonable given absence of all other infection markers, though direct measurement of infectious virus would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Inhalation therapy with recombinant murine soluble ACE2 (rmsACE2) fully protected mice from mCOVID-19. In BALB/c mice, rmsACE2 prevented weight loss, reduced hypothermia, decreased lung weights and viral loads, protected from pneumonia, and reduced blood neutrophils. In C57BL/6 mice, rmsACE2 prevented weight loss and reduced viral load without affecting temperature, lung weight, or blood leukocytes. Therapeutic efficacy was maintained when treatment was initiated 12 hr post-infection, with reduced but significant protection at 24-48 hr post-infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C68-C78 are comprehensively supported by rmsACE2 treatment experiments (Figure 7F-O, supplements) showing dose-dependent and timing-dependent protection in both mouse strains. The data demonstrate both prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, though the therapeutic window appears limited.

results.result: Disease severity in mCOVID-19 is determined by cytokine-driven immunopathology (IFNγ and TNF) and critically dependent on ACE2 in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C8 is supported by converging evidence from cytokine blocking experiments (C5, C56-C62) showing reduced pathology and ACE2 knockout experiments (C6, C63-C67) showing complete protection. This integrates multiple experimental approaches to establish both immunopathology mechanisms and receptor dependency.

results.result: The Q498H mutation was previously engineered by the Baric group for mouse adaptation, and Q493R was found in other mouse-adapted strains. These mutations were rare in human samples until appearing in Omicron/B.1.1.529 (Q493R, Q498R). K417 mutations appeared in Omicron, Beta, and Gamma VOCs. The co-appearance of Q493 and Q498 mutations in Omicron and maVie16 supports the hypothesis of Omicron originating from reverse zoonosis and viral evolution in an animal reservoir.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C115 are supported by citations to previous studies and sequence databases, but the inference about Omicron's origin (C115) is speculative. While the mutation convergence is notable, alternative explanations for Omicron's origin exist, and the claim requires additional evidence beyond mutation similarity. The structural and functional context is well-documented, but the evolutionary inference remains uncertain.

results.result: The time to symptom onset in maVie16-infected mice was approximately 2-3 days, faster than reported in humans (around 5 days), potentially explained by intranasal administration delivering high viral doses to lower airways versus droplet infection of upper respiratory tract in humans.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by comparison of disease kinetics data with cited human data, and the proposed explanation for the difference is mechanistically reasonable. However, this represents a limitation of the model rather than a perfect recapitulation of human disease kinetics.

results.result: IFNs play an ambiguous role during COVID-19, and IFNγ/TNF have been previously associated with severe COVID-19 and PANoptosis in KRT18-hACE2 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 are supported by citations to previous studies. These claims provide context for the current work but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings. The acknowledgment of IFN's ambiguous role appropriately identifies need for future experiments.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence from crystallography, modeling, in vitro experiments, and in vivo studies propose ACE2 as the main SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor, though alternative receptors have been proposed. Human genetic studies, organoid experiments, and animal model studies support ACE2's role and therapeutic potential. ACE2 inhalation has potential to prevent or treat early SARS-CoV-2 infections irrespective of variant, though clinical validation is needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C129 are supported by extensive citations to prior literature and clinical trial data. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study's focus on ACE2. The therapeutic potential claim (C129) is appropriately qualified as requiring clinical validation.

results.result: Background claims establishing COVID-19 epidemiology, clinical features, viral tropism, immunopathology mechanisms, mouse resistance to SARS-CoV-2, limitations of existing mouse models, and general biological knowledge about immune cell functions and disease indicators.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C99, C138-C139 represent established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations to WHO data, clinical studies, and immunology literature. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.
